conversations.relationship_context: An aristocratic bachelor and his manservant discuss piano playing, refreshments, and household champagne.

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 90-91

turns.speaker: LANE
turns.text: I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 93-94

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: I’m sorry for that, for your sake. I don’t play accurately—any one can play accurately—but I play with wonderful expression. As far as the piano is concerned, sentiment is my forte. I keep science for Life.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 96-99

turns.speaker: LANE
turns.text: Yes, sir.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 101-102

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: And, speaking of the science of Life, have you got the cucumber sandwiches cut for Lady Bracknell?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 104-106

turns.speaker: LANE
turns.text: Yes, sir. [Hands them on a salver.]
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 108-109

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: [Inspects them, takes two, and sits down on the sofa.] Oh! . . . by the way, Lane, I see from your book that on Thursday night, when Lord Shoreman and Mr. Worthing were dining with me, eight bottles of champagne are entered as having been consumed.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 111-115

turns.speaker: LANE
turns.text: Yes, sir; eight bottles and a pint.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 117-118

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Why is it that at a bachelor’s establishment the servants invariably drink the champagne? I ask merely for information.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 120-122

turns.speaker: LANE
turns.text: I attribute it to the superior quality of the wine, sir. I have often observed that in married households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate brand.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 124-127

conversations.relationship_context: Two close friends banter about town, country life, and disagreeable neighbors.

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: How are you, my dear Ernest? What brings you up to town?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 166-167

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Oh, pleasure, pleasure! What else should bring one anywhere? Eating as usual, I see, Algy!
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 169-171

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: [Stiffly_._] I believe it is customary in good society to take some slight refreshment at five o’clock. Where have you been since last Thursday?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 173-176

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Sitting down on the sofa.] In the country.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 178-179

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: What on earth do you do there?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 181-182

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Pulling off his gloves_._] When one is in town one amuses oneself. When one is in the country one amuses other people. It is excessively boring.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 184-187

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: And who are the people you amuse?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 189-190

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Airily_._] Oh, neighbours, neighbours.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 192-193

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Got nice neighbours in your part of Shropshire?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 195-196

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Perfectly horrid! Never speak to one of them.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 198-199

conversations.relationship_context: A suitor tries to declare his love while the woman he courts explains her confidence in his supposed name.

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Charming day it has been, Miss Fairfax.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 707-708

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Pray don’t talk to me about the weather, Mr. Worthing. Whenever people talk to me about the weather, I always feel quite certain that they mean something else. And that makes me so nervous.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 710-713

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: I _do_ mean something else.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 715-716

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: I thought so. In fact, I am never wrong.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 718-719

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: And I would like to be allowed to take advantage of Lady Bracknell’s temporary absence . . .
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 721-723

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: I would certainly advise you to do so. Mamma has a way of coming back suddenly into a room that I have often had to speak to her about.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 725-727

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Nervously.] Miss Fairfax, ever since I met you I have admired you more than any girl . . . I have ever met since . . . I met you.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 729-731

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Yes, I am quite well aware of the fact. And I often wish that in public, at any rate, you had been more demonstrative. For me you have always had an irresistible fascination. Even before I met you I was far from indifferent to you. [Jack looks at her in amazement.] We live, as I hope you know, Mr. Worthing, in an age of ideals. The fact is constantly mentioned in the more expensive monthly magazines, and has reached the provincial pulpits, I am told; and my ideal has always been to love some one of the name of Ernest. There is something in that name that inspires absolute confidence. The moment Algernon first mentioned to me that he had a friend called Ernest, I knew I was destined to love you.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 733-744

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: You really love me, Gwendolen?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 746-747

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Passionately!
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 749-750

conversations.relationship_context: A prospective mother-in-law formally interviews her daughter’s suitor about his habits, age, education, and income.

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 890-891

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: [Pencil and note-book in hand.] I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 893-898

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 900-901

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 903-906

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Twenty-nine.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 908-909

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 911-914

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [After some hesitation.] I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 916-917

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 919-926

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 928-929

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: [Makes a note in her book.] In land, or in investments?
turns.source_locator: Act I, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 931-932

conversations.relationship_context: A governess urges her ward to study German while the ward comments on her guardian and keeps a diary.

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: [Calling.] Cecily, Cecily! Surely such a utilitarian occupation as the watering of flowers is rather Moulton’s duty than yours? Especially at a moment when intellectual pleasures await you. Your German grammar is on the table. Pray open it at page fifteen. We will repeat yesterday’s lesson.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1426-1431

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: [Coming over very slowly.] But I don’t like German. It isn’t at all a becoming language. I know perfectly well that I look quite plain after my German lesson.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1433-1436

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: Child, you know how anxious your guardian is that you should improve yourself in every way. He laid particular stress on your German, as he was leaving for town yesterday. Indeed, he always lays stress on your German when he is leaving for town.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1438-1442

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Dear Uncle Jack is so very serious! Sometimes he is so serious that I think he cannot be quite well.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1444-1446

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: [Drawing herself up.] Your guardian enjoys the best of health, and his gravity of demeanour is especially to be commended in one so comparatively young as he is. I know no one who has a higher sense of duty and responsibility.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1448-1452

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I suppose that is why he often looks a little bored when we three are together.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1454-1456

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: Cecily! I am surprised at you. Mr. Worthing has many troubles in his life. Idle merriment and triviality would be out of place in his conversation. You must remember his constant anxiety about that unfortunate young man his brother.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1458-1462

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I wish Uncle Jack would allow that unfortunate young man, his brother, to come down here sometimes. We might have a good influence over him, Miss Prism. I am sure you certainly would. You know German, and geology, and things of that kind influence a man very much. [Cecily begins to write in her diary.]
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1464-1469

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: [Shaking her head.] I do not think that even I could produce any effect on a character that according to his own brother’s admission is irretrievably weak and vacillating. Indeed I am not sure that I would desire to reclaim him. I am not in favour of this modern mania for turning bad people into good people at a moment’s notice. As a man sows so let him reap. You must put away your diary, Cecily. I really don’t see why you should keep a diary at all.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1471-1478

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I keep a diary in order to enter the wonderful secrets of my life. If I didn’t write them down, I should probably forget all about them.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1480-1482

conversations.relationship_context: Two supposed cousins meet for the first time while one is using a false identity and the other tests his claimed wickedness.

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: [Raising his hat.] You are my little cousin Cecily, I’m sure.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1616-1617

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: You are under some strange mistake. I am not little. In fact, I believe I am more than usually tall for my age. [Algernon is rather taken aback.] But I am your cousin Cecily. You, I see from your card, are Uncle Jack’s brother, my cousin Ernest, my wicked cousin Ernest.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1619-1623

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Oh! I am not really wicked at all, cousin Cecily. You mustn’t think that I am wicked.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1625-1627

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: If you are not, then you have certainly been deceiving us all in a very inexcusable manner. I hope you have not been leading a double life, pretending to be wicked and being really good all the time. That would be hypocrisy.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1629-1633

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: [Looks at her in amazement.] Oh! Of course I have been rather reckless.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1635-1636

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I am glad to hear it.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1638-1639

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: In fact, now you mention the subject, I have been very bad in my own small way.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1641-1643

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I don’t think you should be so proud of that, though I am sure it must have been very pleasant.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1645-1647

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: It is much pleasanter being here with you.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1649-1650

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I can’t understand how you are here at all. Uncle Jack won’t be back till Monday afternoon.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1652-1654

conversations.relationship_context: A guardian in mourning tells a clergyman and governess that his fictitious brother has died.

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Shakes Miss Prism’s hand in a tragic manner.] I have returned sooner than I expected. Dr. Chasuble, I hope you are well?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1812-1814

turns.speaker: CHASUBLE
turns.text: Dear Mr. Worthing, I trust this garb of woe does not betoken some terrible calamity?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1816-1818

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: My brother.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1820-1821

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: More shameful debts and extravagance?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1823-1824

turns.speaker: CHASUBLE
turns.text: Still leading his life of pleasure?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1826-1827

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Shaking his head.] Dead!
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1829-1830

turns.speaker: CHASUBLE
turns.text: Your brother Ernest dead?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1832-1833

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Quite dead.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1835-1836

turns.speaker: MISS PRISM
turns.text: What a lesson for him! I trust he will profit by it.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1838-1839

turns.speaker: CHASUBLE
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, I offer you my sincere condolence. You have at least the consolation of knowing that you were always the most generous and forgiving of brothers.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 1841-1844

conversations.relationship_context: Newly acquainted romantic interests discuss an impending departure until a servant announces the waiting carriage.

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Oh, I merely came back to water the roses. I thought you were with Uncle Jack.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2184-2186

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: He’s gone to order the dog-cart for me.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2188-2189

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Oh, is he going to take you for a nice drive?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2191-2192

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: He’s going to send me away.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2194-2195

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Then have we got to part?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2197-2198

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: I am afraid so. It’s a very painful parting.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2200-2201

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: It is always painful to part from people whom one has known for a very brief space of time. The absence of old friends one can endure with equanimity. But even a momentary separation from anyone to whom one has just been introduced is almost unbearable.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2203-2207

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Thank you.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2209-2210

turns.speaker: MERRIMAN
turns.text: The dog-cart is at the door, sir. [Algernon looks appealingly at Cecily.]
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2214-2216

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: It can wait, Merriman for . . . five minutes.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2218-2219

conversations.relationship_context: Two apparent new friends become uneasy while trying to determine which man named Ernest is connected to each of them.

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Pray do! I think that whenever one has anything unpleasant to say, one should always be quite candid.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2576-2578

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Well, to speak with perfect candour, Cecily, I wish that you were fully forty-two, and more than usually plain for your age. Ernest has a strong upright nature. He is the very soul of truth and honour. Disloyalty would be as impossible to him as deception. But even men of the noblest possible moral character are extremely susceptible to the influence of the physical charms of others. Modern, no less than Ancient History, supplies us with many most painful examples of what I refer to. If it were not so, indeed, History would be quite unreadable.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2580-2588

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I beg your pardon, Gwendolen, did you say Ernest?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2590-2591

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Yes.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2593-2594

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Oh, but it is not Mr. Ernest Worthing who is my guardian. It is his brother—his elder brother.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2596-2598

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: [Sitting down again.] Ernest never mentioned to me that he had a brother.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2600-2602

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: I am sorry to say they have not been on good terms for a long time.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2604-2605

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Ah! that accounts for it. And now that I think of it I have never heard any man mention his brother. The subject seems distasteful to most men. Cecily, you have lifted a load from my mind. I was growing almost anxious. It would have been terrible if any cloud had come across a friendship like ours, would it not? Of course you are quite, quite sure that it is not Mr. Ernest Worthing who is your guardian?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2607-2613

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: Quite sure. [A pause.] In fact, I am going to be his.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2615-2616

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: [Inquiringly.] I beg your pardon?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2618-2619

conversations.relationship_context: Two friends and romantic rivals accuse each other of deception after their false identities are exposed.

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: This ghastly state of things is what you call Bunburying, I suppose?
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2921-2922

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Yes, and a perfectly wonderful Bunbury it is. The most wonderful Bunbury I have ever had in my life.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2924-2926

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Well, you’ve no right whatsoever to Bunbury here.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2928-2929

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: That is absurd. One has a right to Bunbury anywhere one chooses. Every serious Bunburyist knows that.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2931-2933

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Serious Bunburyist! Good heavens!
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2935-2936

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Well, one must be serious about something, if one wants to have any amusement in life. I happen to be serious about Bunburying. What on earth you are serious about I haven’t got the remotest idea. About everything, I should fancy. You have such an absolutely trivial nature.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2938-2942

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Well, the only small satisfaction I have in the whole of this wretched business is that your friend Bunbury is quite exploded. You won’t be able to run down to the country quite so often as you used to do, dear Algy. And a very good thing too.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2944-2948

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: Your brother is a little off colour, isn’t he, dear Jack? You won’t be able to disappear to London quite so frequently as your wicked custom was. And not a bad thing either.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2950-2953

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: As for your conduct towards Miss Cardew, I must say that your taking in a sweet, simple, innocent girl like that is quite inexcusable. To say nothing of the fact that she is my ward.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2955-2958

turns.speaker: ALGERNON
turns.text: I can see no possible defence at all for your deceiving a brilliant, clever, thoroughly experienced young lady like Miss Fairfax. To say nothing of the fact that she is my cousin.
turns.source_locator: Act II, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 2960-2963

conversations.relationship_context: Two friends privately observe their apologetic suitors and agree to maintain a dignified silence.

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: The fact that they did not follow us at once into the house, as any one else would have done, seems to me to show that they have some sense of shame left.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3108-3111

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: They have been eating muffins. That looks like repentance.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3113-3114

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: [After a pause.] They don’t seem to notice us at all. Couldn’t you cough?
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3116-3118

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: But I haven’t got a cough.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3120-3121

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: They’re looking at us. What effrontery!
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3123-3124

turns.speaker: CECILY
turns.text: They’re approaching. That’s very forward of them.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3126-3127

turns.speaker: GWENDOLEN
turns.text: Let us preserve a dignified silence.

turns.speaker: CECILY

conversations.relationship_context: A guardian answers an aristocratic aunt’s investigation into his ward’s family credentials and fortune.

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [In a clear, cold voice.] Miss Cardew is the grand-daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Cardew of 149 Belgrave Square, S.W.; Gervase Park, Dorking, Surrey; and the Sporran, Fifeshire, N.B.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3351-3354

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: That sounds not unsatisfactory. Three addresses always inspire confidence, even in tradesmen. But what proof have I of their authenticity?
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3356-3359

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: I have carefully preserved the Court Guides of the period. They are open to your inspection, Lady Bracknell.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3361-3363

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: [Grimly.] I have known strange errors in that publication.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3365-3366

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Miss Cardew’s family solicitors are Messrs. Markby, Markby, and Markby.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3368-3369

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: Markby, Markby, and Markby? A firm of the very highest position in their profession. Indeed I am told that one of the Mr. Markby’s is occasionally to be seen at dinner parties. So far I am satisfied.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3371-3374

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: [Very irritably.] How extremely kind of you, Lady Bracknell! I have also in my possession, you will be pleased to hear, certificates of Miss Cardew’s birth, baptism, whooping cough, registration, vaccination, confirmation, and the measles; both the German and the English variety.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3376-3381

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: Ah! A life crowded with incident, I see; though perhaps somewhat too exciting for a young girl. I am not myself in favour of premature experiences. [Rises, looks at her watch.] Gwendolen! the time approaches for our departure. We have not a moment to lose. As a matter of form, Mr. Worthing, I had better ask you if Miss Cardew has any little fortune?
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3383-3389

turns.speaker: JACK
turns.text: Oh! about a hundred and thirty thousand pounds in the Funds. That is all. Goodbye, Lady Bracknell. So pleased to have seen you.
turns.source_locator: Act III, Project Gutenberg plain-text lines 3391-3393

turns.speaker: LADY BRACKNELL
turns.text: [Sitting down again.] A moment, Mr. Worthing. A hundred and thirty thousand pounds! And in the Funds! Miss Cardew seems to me a most attractive young lady, now that I look at her. Few girls of the present day have any really solid qualities, any of the qualities that last, and improve with time. We live, I regret to say, in an age of surfaces. [To Cecily.] Come over here, dear. [Cecily goes across.] Pretty child! your dress is sadly simple, and your hair seems almost as Nature might have left it. But we can soon alter all that. A thoroughly experienced French maid produces a really marvellous result in a very brief space of time. I remember recommending one to young Lady Lancing, and after three months her own husband did not know her.
